goal_text: How to do good user research

nodes.title: What user research actually is (and isn't)
nodes.one_liner: Why we research users, and what it can and can't tell you.

nodes.title: Start with the right question
nodes.one_liner: Turning a vague goal into a focused research question.

nodes.title: Generative vs. evaluative research
nodes.one_liner: The two main reasons to research, and when to use each.

nodes.title: Pick a method that fits the question
nodes.one_liner: Interviews, observation, surveys, tests — and choosing among them.

nodes.title: Find and recruit the right people
nodes.one_liner: Who to talk to, how many, and how to reach them.

nodes.title: Run a good interview or session
nodes.one_liner: Asking questions that get honest, useful answers.

nodes.title: Avoid bias that ruins your findings
nodes.one_liner: Leading questions, small samples, and fooling yourself.

nodes.title: Turn raw notes into real insights
nodes.one_liner: Spotting patterns and synthesizing what you heard.

nodes.title: Make findings actually change decisions
nodes.one_liner: Sharing results so they get used, not shelved.

outline.rationale: The user is a total beginner wanting a solid conceptual-but-practical working understanding, no specific deliverable. I built the outline around the full arc of research: framing (what it is, asking the right question), the key conceptual fork (generative vs evaluative), method selection, recruiting, execution (running sessions), a dedicated bias node (critical for beginners and the most common failure mode), synthesis, and impact. I excluded an intro node, heavy quantitative/statistics, and research ops per the confirmed scope. Nodes are MECE-ish: framing, method choice, recruiting, doing, validity, analysis, and dissemination have low content overlap. Order follows the natural dependency chain while keeping each node distinct.
